hints: Count carefully from the displayed structure, remember each phenolic $\text{OH}$, the side chain $\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ and the three remaining H atoms on the disubstituted benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Build the atom count piece by piece**
Look at the picture with me. The benzene ring gives you $6$ carbons, plus $2$ carbons in the $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ side chain, so $8$ carbons in total. For hydrogen, the ring has $3$ H left after three substitutions, the two phenolic $\text{OH}$ groups give $2$ H, the $\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ gives $1+1$ H, the $\text{CH}_{2}$ gives $2$ H and the $\text{NH}_{2}$ gives $2$ H, total $11$ H. With $1$ N and $3$ O atoms, you get $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{3}$.
Final answer: Molecular formula of noradrenaline is $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{3}$.

hints: Focus on the benzylic carbon bearing the $\text{OH}$ group and check whether its four attached groups are all different.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre**
Find the carbon with the side chain $\text{OH}$, the $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ carbon. It is attached to four different things: $\text{OH}$, H, the 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl ring, and the $-\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ group. No plane of symmetry there, so that carbon is chiral.

Link chirality to optical activity**
One chiral centre means the molecule exists as a pair of non superimposable mirror images, enantiomers, which rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions. That is exactly what optical isomerism means.
Final answer: Yes, noradrenaline shows optical isomerism as it contains a chiral carbon atom bonded to four different groups.

hints: Compare what happens to a positive charge next to a benzene ring versus next to an alkyl chain, think about overlap with the pi system.
walkthrough:
Picture the two diazonium ions**
When phenylamine reacts with $\text{HNO}_{2}$ at $0$ to $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ you get $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}$, with $-\text{N}_{2}^{+}$ directly attached to the ring. When noradrenaline, an aliphatic primary amine, reacts you get an alkyl $-\text{N}_{2}^{+}$ with no ring conjugation.

See why the ring helps**
Next to the benzene ring the positive charge on nitrogen can interact with the delocalised pi electrons of the ring, so the charge is spread, delocalised, over the ring. Spreading charge always lowers energy and increases stability. With no ring to share the charge, the aliphatic diazonium ion stays localised, very unstable, and immediately loses $\text{N}_{2}$.
Final answer: The benzenediazonium ion is stabilised because the positive charge is delocalised over the benzene ring.

hints: Recall the general reaction of a primary aliphatic amine $\text{RNH}_{2}$ with $\text{HNO}_{2}$, what replaces the $-\text{NH}_{2}$ group and what gas is evolved?
Apply that to noradrenaline, keep the 3,4-dihydroxybenzene ring and the benzylic $\text{OH}$ unchanged and change only $-\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ to $-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
Remember the aliphatic amine pattern**
For $\text{R-NH}_{2} + \text{HNO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{R-OH} + \text{N}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, the unstable alkyldiazonium ion loses nitrogen gas and the carbocation is captured by water to give an alcohol. So $-\text{NH}_{2}$ is effectively replaced by $-\text{OH}$.

Draw the C, H, O only product**
Leave the whole 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl part alone. Leave the benzylic $\text{CH}(\text{OH})$ alone. Just convert $-\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ into $-\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. Your box should show a benzene ring with two adjacent $\text{OH}$ groups and a $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ side chain. That molecule contains only C, H and O.

Complete the equation**
The missing small molecule is nitrogen, $\text{N}_{2}$, from decomposition of the diazonium group. So the full balanced form is: $$\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{3} + \text{HNO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{4} + \text{N}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

Final answer: Organic product is $3,4\text{-(HO)}_{2}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ : benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ groups at 3 and 4 positions attached to $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.
Equation: noradrenaline + $\text{HNO}_{2} \rightarrow$ diol + $\text{N}_{2}$ + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.
